title: The Andersens
headline: Live Oak Ridge House: a courtyard in limestone and shade
summary: A one-story courtyard house in Dripping Springs that turns its back to the west sun and opens to live oaks, a garden court, and summer rain.
challenge: The Andersens bought two acres of oak and limestone and a view they loved — facing due west. The brief was a house that stayed cool without hiding indoors, with room for adult children and a studio for pottery.
approach:
I arranged the house as a shallow U around a courtyard: living spaces on the north arm, bedrooms on the south, and a low studio closing the west with a solid limestone wall and one high window. Deep porches, a standing-seam roof that harvests rain, and windows placed for cross-breezes do most of the cooling before the system ever starts.

Every room looks into the court or under an oak. None looks into the sunset.
results:
38°|cooler courtyard at 6 pm in August (modeled)
100%|of rooms with cross-ventilation
2|live oaks kept within the courtyard
1|architect, first sketch to final walk
stack: Local limestone, standing-seam metal, cypress, polished concrete
quote: Elena walked the land four times before she drew a line. The house sits exactly where she stood.

title: The Okafor Family
headline: Casita Verde: a garden ADU that earns its keep
summary: A 640-square-foot garden house in Hyde Park for a parent now, a studio next, and a rental someday — without cutting the heritage oak.
challenge: The Okafors needed a home for a parent close to the main house, on a lot governed by a heritage oak and Austin's ADU rules. Three futures had to fit in one small plan.
approach: The casita tucks under the oak's drip line on pier-and-beam, with a kitchen that can close off, a bath that works at any age, and a porch that faces the garden, not the alley. Plumbing stacks so a future rental conversion takes a weekend, not a remodel.
results:
640 sq ft|one bedroom, full kitchen and bath
0|heritage trees removed
3|future uses in one plan
14 ft|from back door to back door
stack: Fiber-cement, standing-seam roof, oak floors, lime plaster
quote: It feels like its own house, not an afterthought. My mother has her garden, and we have our evenings.

title: Marta and Luis Herrera
headline: Barton Hills Ranch, opened to the garden
summary: A 1968 ranch that kept its brick, its roofline and its soul — and lost the walls that kept it dark.
challenge: The Herreras loved their street and their brick ranch, but the kitchen faced a wall and the garden might as well have been a photograph. Moving was priced; so was a teardown.
approach: We kept the shell and the roof, removed two walls, and cut a 16-foot opening to a new shaded porch. The kitchen moved to the light, a mudroom caught the daily mess, and the primary bath borrowed space from a closet that held only luggage.
results:
2|walls removed, 0 additions to the footprint
16 ft|new opening to the porch
1968|original brick and roof kept
9 months|lived nearby, not in a teardown
stack: Original brick, white oak, steel, shaded aluminum porch
quote: People ask if we moved. We tell them we just finally met our garden.

title: June Park
headline: Wimberley Courtyard House for the next chapter
summary: A 1,450-square-foot house for retirement: one level, no hallways wasted, a courtyard for reading and grandchildren.
challenge: June wanted to leave a two-story house without leaving the Hill Country. Everything on one level, maintenance she could manage, and a place that felt generous at half the size.
approach: Rooms wrap a small court with a fountain that masks the road. Thick walls, small west windows, and a gallery that doubles as library keep it quiet and cool. The guest room is also the studio, with a door to the court.
results:
1,450 sq ft|two bedrooms, no stairs
0|hallways (rooms open to the gallery)
1|courtyard, visible from every room
68 dB → 41 dB|road noise inside (modeled)
stack: Limestone veneer, metal roof, douglas fir, concrete
quote: I downsized everything except how it feels to be home.

title: The Delgados
headline: Fredericksburg House of deep shade
summary: A Hill Country house of limestone piers and a big roof, built for harvest weekends and hot Septembers.
challenge: The Delgados gather three generations for peach season. They needed shade at noon, beds for twelve, and a house that belonged to its limestone ridge.
approach: A single big roof floats over limestone piers and glass between them. Sleeping lofts flank a great room that opens on two sides; when the doors slide away, the ridge breeze does the rest.
results:
12|beds without a single bunk room
24 ft|of sliding glass, two sides
100%|rain harvested for landscape
3|generations under one roof
stack: Limestone piers, steel, glass, metal roof
quote: At noon in September we eat outside. That was the whole design, really.

title: Samira Khan
headline: A writer's casita in Zilker
summary: A 480-square-foot studio ADU where a novelist writes, a guest sleeps, and the bungalow keeps its yard.
challenge: Samira needed quiet that a spare room could not give, plus a guest bed twice a year. The yard was small and the bungalow's charm was non-negotiable.
approach: The casita reads as a garden shed from the street and a small house from inside: a writing desk under a north window, a Murphy bed, a bath, and just enough kitchen for tea and deadlines.
results:
480 sq ft|studio, bath, kitchenette
1|north window over the desk
2|uses: writing daily, guests rarely
0|inches of bungalow altered
stack: Cedar, metal roof, north glass, lime wash
quote: I finished a novel in that room. The north light alone was worth it.
